chapters.title: Logic and proof

maps.title: Logic
links: Implication | is false only | True implies false
Induction | proves | Statements for all n

summary: Logic is the grammar of mathematics and of programs. A proposition is a statement that is true or false. Connectives such as and, or, not and implies build new propositions from old ones, and truth tables say exactly when they hold.

Quantifiers say for all and there exists. Proofs are arguments that a statement must hold: direct proof, proof by contradiction, and mathematical induction, which proves a statement for every natural number.
Every later chapter relies on these tools. The labs evaluate formulas, check tautologies and prove a sum formula by testing it.

glossary.def: A statement that is either true or false.
p implies q is false only when p is true and q is false.
A formula true under every assignment of its variables.
For all (universal) or there exists (existential).
Prove a base case, and that each case implies the next.
Not q implies not p; equivalent to p implies q.

keyPoints: Connectives: not, and, or, implies, if and only if.
p implies q is equivalent to (not p) or q, and to its contrapositive.
De Morgan: not (p and q) = (not p) or (not q); not (p or q) = (not p) and (not q).
Negating for all gives there exists not; negating there exists gives for all not.
Induction: P(0) and (P(n) implies P(n+1)) give P(n) for all n.
Strong induction assumes P(k) for all k below n.

items: ELI5. Logic is the rules of a fair argument. Imagine a promise: if it rains, I will bring an umbrella. The promise is only broken if it rains and I forget. Proof by induction is a line of dominoes: knock the first, and each one knocks the next.

A proposition is a sentence that is either true or false, like 7 is prime. We combine propositions with connectives. And is true when both parts are. Or is true when at least one is. Not flips the value. The most important and most misunderstood connective is implication.

The statement p implies q is false in exactly one case: p true and q false. If p is false the implication is true whatever q is. This is called vacuous truth. The statement is equivalent to not p or q.
It is also equivalent to its contrapositive, not q implies not p, but not to its converse, q implies p.

lesson.tex:
egin{gathered} 
eg(p \wedge q) \equiv 
eg p \vee 
eg q, \[0.6em] 
eg(p \vee q) \equiv 
eg p \wedge 
eg q, \[0.6em] p \Rightarrow q \equiv 
eg p \vee q \end{gathered}

items: Quantifiers add generality. For all x in a set, P of x says that P holds for every element. There exists x such that P of x says some element works. To negate a quantified statement, swap the quantifier and negate the body. The negation of every swan is white is some swan is not white.
Proof techniques turn these into arguments. A direct proof assumes the hypothesis and derives the conclusion. Proof by contradiction assumes the conclusion is false and derives an absurdity.
Proof by induction handles statements about all natural numbers: prove the case for zero, then prove that if the case for n holds, so does the case for n plus one.

As an example, the formula above holds for n equal to one, since both sides are one. If it holds for n, adding n plus one to both sides gives the formula for n plus one. Induction is the logical twin of recursion: a recursive function and an inductive proof have the same shape.
Later, in the type theory chapter, you will see that this resemblance is exact.

chapters.title: Sets, relations and functions

maps.title: Sets
links: Relation | is | A set of pairs

summary: A set is a collection of distinct things. Sets have union, intersection and complement; the Cartesian product forms pairs. A relation is a set of pairs, and a function is a relation that gives exactly one output for each input.

Injective functions never merge inputs, surjective ones hit every output, and bijective ones are both and so can be inverted. Equivalence relations split a set into disjoint classes, which is how we define things like integers modulo n.
The labs implement set operations, compose functions and test properties of relations.

glossary.def: An unordered collection of distinct elements.
A x B is the set of pairs (a, b).
A subset of a Cartesian product.
A relation with exactly one output per input.
One-to-one; onto; both.
Reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

keyPoints: |A union B| = |A| + |B| - |A intersect B|.
|A x B| = |A| |B|; a set of n elements has 2^n subsets.
A function f: A -> B has one output per input.
f is invertible exactly when it is a bijection.
Equivalence: reflexive, symmetric, transitive; its classes partition the set.
Composition: (g o f)(x) = g(f(x)).

items: ELI5. A set is a bag where each item appears once. A function is a machine that gives exactly one answer for each input. A bijection is a perfect pairing, like every guest with exactly one seat and every seat with one guest.

Sets are the basic language. We write membership as x in A. Two sets are equal when they have the same elements, and order and repetition do not matter. The power set of A is the set of all subsets of A, and has two to the n elements when A has n.

A relation from A to B is a subset of the product A times B. Less than on the integers is a relation. A function is a special relation in which each input has exactly one output. We write f from A to B. The set A is the domain and B the codomain. The image is the set of outputs actually reached.

Three properties matter. A function is injective if different inputs give different outputs. It is surjective if every element of the codomain is an output. It is bijective if it is both, in which case an inverse function exists.
Bijections between sets show they have the same size, which is how we compare infinite sizes.

An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. It groups elements into equivalence classes, and the classes partition the set. Congruence modulo n is an equivalence relation on the integers, and its classes are the residues zero to n minus one.

In computing, sets are the model for types and collections, functions are the model of programs, and relations model databases. Later chapters on category theory and type theory start from functions and ask what can be said using only composition.

chapters.title: Counting and combinatorics
summary: Counting is the maths behind complexity, probability and hashing. The product rule multiplies independent choices; the sum rule adds disjoint cases. A permutation orders items; a combination picks a subset.

The number of ways to choose k of n items is the binomial coefficient n choose k. The pigeonhole principle says that more items than boxes forces a box with two, and inclusion-exclusion corrects for overlaps.
The labs compute factorials, binomials, derangement-style counts and the birthday collision probability.

glossary.def: n! = n (n-1) ... 1, the number of orderings of n items.
An ordered arrangement; P(n, k) = n!/(n-k)!.
An unordered choice; C(n, k) = n!/(k!(n-k)!).
(x + y)^n = sum C(n, k) x^k y^(n-k).
n + 1 items in n boxes: some box has two.
Add singles, subtract pairs, add triples, and so on.

keyPoints: C(n, k) = C(n-1, k-1) + C(n-1, k) (Pascal).
Sum of C(n, k) over k equals 2^n.
Pigeonhole: if more than n items go into n boxes, some box holds at least two.
Birthday problem: collisions appear after about sqrt(n) draws from n values.
Stars and bars: ways to split n identical items into k groups is C(n+k-1, k-1).

items: ELI5. Counting is about how many choices you have. Three shirts and four trousers make twelve outfits: multiply. Choosing a team of three from ten, where order does not matter, divides out the repeated orderings.

How many passwords of length four use the digits zero to nine? Each of four positions has ten options, independent of the others, so the product rule gives ten to the fourth, or 10,000. If the options depend on the case, split into disjoint cases and add: the sum rule.

Ordering matters in permutations. Arranging n different items gives n factorial orderings: n choices for the first place, n minus one for the next, and so on. Picking and ordering k of n gives n times n minus one down to n minus k plus one.

When order does not matter, divide out the orderings: n choose k counts the subsets of size k. The recurrence is Pascal's rule and builds Pascal's triangle. Summing a row gives two to the n, the number of all subsets, matching the power set of the last chapter.

The pigeonhole principle is simple and powerful: put more than n items into n boxes and some box holds two. It proves that any lossless compressor must enlarge some inputs. A probabilistic cousin is the birthday problem: among only 23 people, two share a birthday with probability above one half.
Collisions in hash tables appear after about the square root of the table size.

Inclusion-exclusion counts a union: add the sizes of the sets, subtract the pairwise overlaps, add back triple overlaps, and so on. We will meet all of this again as the foundation of discrete probability.

chapters.title: Graphs, trees and relations as graphs

maps.title: Graphs
links: Degree | counts | Edges at a vertex
Tree | is | A connected acyclic graph

summary: A graph is a set of vertices joined by edges. Graphs model networks, dependencies, states and relations. Degree counts the edges at a vertex, and the handshake lemma says the degrees add up to twice the number of edges.
A tree is a connected graph without cycles; a tree on n vertices has n minus 1 edges. Graphs are stored as adjacency lists or matrices and explored with breadth-first or depth-first search.
The labs build adjacency structures, count degrees, test for trees and run a breadth-first search.

glossary.def: A set of vertices V and edges E.
The number of edges at a vertex.
A walk without repeated vertices; a closed path.
A connected graph with no cycle.
A matrix A with A[i][j] = 1 when there is an edge i to j.
A maximal set of mutually reachable vertices.

keyPoints: Sum of degrees = 2 |E| (handshake lemma).
A tree on n vertices has n - 1 edges and a unique path between any two vertices.
A connected graph on n vertices has at least n - 1 edges.
Powers of the adjacency matrix count walks: (A^k)[i][j] is the number of walks of length k.
BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
A directed acyclic graph can be topologically ordered.

items: ELI5. A graph is dots joined by lines, like friends on a map. A tree is a graph with no loops, like a family tree. Counting each friendship at both ends explains why the total of friends is twice the number of friendships.

A graph consists of vertices and edges. Roads, social networks, the links of a web, the dependencies between software packages and the states of an automaton are all graphs. An edge may be undirected or directed, and may carry a weight.

The degree of a vertex is the number of edges at it. Every edge contributes to two degrees, so the sum of all degrees is twice the number of edges. This handshake lemma implies that the number of odd-degree vertices is even.

A path is a sequence of vertices linked by edges. A graph is connected if a path joins every pair of vertices. A tree is a connected graph with no cycles. Trees on n vertices always have exactly n minus one edges, and between any two vertices there is exactly one path.
Rooted trees organise hierarchies: file systems, syntax trees, search trees.
To compute with graphs we store them. An adjacency list gives each vertex its neighbours and is compact for sparse graphs. An adjacency matrix has a one at row i, column j when there is an edge.
A nice fact links it to linear algebra: the k-th power of the matrix counts the walks of length k between each pair of vertices.

Breadth-first search explores outward in layers and finds shortest paths when edges have equal cost. Depth-first search dives deep before backtracking and underlies topological sorting and cycle detection. The data structures and algorithms course covers them in full.
Here we use graphs as a language for relations.

practice.intro: Write bfs_dist(n, edges, s, t): the number of edges on a shortest path from s to t in an undirected graph, or -1 if unreachable.
practice.solution:
def bfs_dist(n, edges, s, t):
    adj = [[] for i in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
        adj[v].append(u)
    dist = [-1] * n
    dist[s] = 0
    q = [s]
    i = 0
    while i < len(q):
        x = q[i]
        i += 1
        for y in adj[x]:
            if dist[y] < 0:
                dist[y] = dist[x] + 1
                q.append(y)
    return dist[t]

chapters.title: Number theory and modular arithmetic

maps.title: Number theory
links: Modular arithmetic | wraps | Around a modulus
Fermat | gives | Fast powers and inverses

summary: Number theory studies integers. Divisibility, primes and the greatest common divisor underlie hashing, random number generators and cryptography. Modular arithmetic, which wraps numbers around a modulus, is arithmetic on a clock.

Euclid's algorithm computes the greatest common divisor quickly. Fast exponentiation computes large powers modulo n, and Fermat's little theorem gives modular inverses for a prime modulus. These tools make public-key cryptography possible.
The labs implement gcd, modular exponentiation, the sieve of Eratosthenes and modular inverses.

glossary.def: a divides b when b = a k for an integer k.
The greatest common divisor of two numbers.
a is congruent to b mod n when n divides a - b.
An integer above 1 with only 1 and itself as divisors.
x with a x congruent to 1 mod n; exists when gcd(a, n) = 1.
For prime p and a not divisible by p: a^(p-1) is congruent to 1 mod p.

keyPoints: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b); gcd(a, 0) = a.
Modular arithmetic respects + and x: (a + b) mod n = ((a mod n) + (b mod n)) mod n.
Square-and-multiply computes a^e mod n in O(log e) steps.
Fermat: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p, so a^(-1) = a^(p-2) mod p.
Every integer above 1 factors uniquely into primes.
RSA's security rests on the difficulty of factoring large products of primes.

items: ELI5. Modular arithmetic is clock arithmetic. Ten o'clock plus five hours is three o'clock, because the numbers wrap around. Computers use it to scramble and to lock secrets, because wrapping around is easy to do but hard to undo.

We say a divides b if b is a times some integer. Every integer greater than one is either prime, with no divisors but one and itself, or a product of primes in a unique way. The greatest common divisor of two numbers is the largest number dividing both.
Euclid, two thousand years ago, found how to compute it quickly.
The rule works because any common divisor of a and b also divides a mod b. Each step shrinks the numbers fast: the algorithm runs in time proportional to the number of digits.

Modular arithmetic works with remainders. We say a is congruent to b modulo n when n divides the difference. Addition and multiplication respect this: you may reduce at any point. Hours on a clock add modulo twelve. Hash functions and checksums use it constantly.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p \\[0.6em] (p \text{ prime},\ p \nmid a), \\[0.6em] a^{-1} \equiv a^{p-2} \pmod p \end{gathered}

items: Large powers are computed by repeated squaring: to find a to the e, square a repeatedly and multiply in the squares that match the binary digits of e. This needs only a logarithmic number of multiplications, each reduced modulo n so the numbers stay small.
Fermat's little theorem then provides modular inverses when n is prime.

Public-key cryptography builds on this. RSA multiplies two large primes to make a public modulus. Anyone can encrypt with modular powers, but undoing it appears to require factoring the modulus. The same ideas give hash tables, pseudo-random generators and error-correcting codes.

chapters.title: Linear algebra I: vectors and matrices
summary: Linear algebra is the language of data and of neural networks. A vector is a list of numbers, a point or an arrow in space. The dot product measures how aligned two vectors are, and the norm measures length.

A matrix is a table of numbers and also a linear map: it turns vectors into vectors. Multiplying matrices composes maps. Almost every layer of a neural network is a matrix multiplication followed by a simple nonlinear function.
The labs implement dot products, norms, cosine similarity, matrix-vector and matrix-matrix products and the transpose.

glossary.def: An ordered list of numbers, an element of R^n.
x . y = sum x_i y_i = |x||y| cos(theta).
|x| = sqrt(x . x): the length of a vector.
A rectangular array that represents a linear map.
(AB)_ij = sum_k A_ik B_kj; composition of maps.
Swap rows and columns: (A^T)_ij = A_ji.

keyPoints: Dot product: x . y = |x||y| cos(theta); zero for orthogonal vectors.
Cauchy-Schwarz: |x . y| <= |x||y|.
Matrix product is associative but not commutative.
(AB)^T = B^T A^T.
A linear map satisfies f(ax + by) = a f(x) + b f(y).
Cosine similarity = (x . y)/(|x||y|), used to compare embeddings.

items: ELI5. A vector is an arrow, or just a list of numbers. The dot product says how much two arrows point the same way. A matrix is a machine that turns arrows into arrows, such as turning or stretching them.

A vector is a list of n numbers. We can add vectors and scale them, and these two operations are what make linear algebra linear. Geometrically a vector in two or three dimensions is an arrow. In machine learning a vector is a data point, an embedding or a set of weights.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} x \cdot y \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i \;=\; \lVert x\rVert\,\lVert y\rVert \cos\theta, \\[0.6em] \lVert x \rVert = \sqrt{x\cdot x} \end{gathered}

items: The dot product multiplies matching entries and adds them. It equals the product of the lengths and the cosine of the angle between the vectors. If it is zero the vectors are orthogonal.
Dividing by the lengths gives the cosine similarity, a measure of alignment between embeddings that ignores their size.

A matrix with m rows and n columns defines a linear map from vectors of length n to vectors of length m. The map sends x to A x, where each output entry is the dot product of a row with x. Rotations, scalings and projections are all matrices.

The product of two matrices corresponds to doing one map after the other. The order matters: A times B is usually not B times A. The sizes must match, with the columns of A equal to the rows of B. Matrix multiplication is associative, which lets us regroup long chains of layers.

Look at a neural-network layer: the output is a nonlinear function of W x plus b, with a weight matrix W. A whole batch of inputs is a matrix and is processed by one large multiplication, which GPUs do very fast. This is why linear algebra is at the heart of deep learning.

chapters.title: Linear algebra II: systems, determinants, eigenvalues and SVD

maps.title: Eigen
links: Linear system | is | A x = b

summary: A linear system A x = b asks which input x the matrix A maps to b. Gaussian elimination solves it by row operations. The determinant tells how a matrix scales volume and whether it can be inverted.

An eigenvector of A is a direction the matrix only stretches; the stretch factor is its eigenvalue. The singular value decomposition factors any matrix into rotations and a stretch, and powers principal component analysis and low-rank compression.
The labs solve systems, compute determinants, find a dominant eigenvalue by power iteration and project data onto a direction.

glossary.def: Equations A x = b with unknown vector x.
A number det(A): the volume scale of the map; zero means not invertible.
A^-1 with A A^-1 = I; exists when det(A) is not zero.
A nonzero v with A v = lambda v.
A = U S V^T with orthogonal U, V and a diagonal S of singular values.
Find directions of greatest variance in data.

keyPoints: Gaussian elimination solves A x = b in O(n^3) operations.
det(AB) = det(A) det(B); det of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal.
A v = lambda v; det(A - lambda I) = 0 gives the eigenvalues.
Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors.
SVD: A = U S V^T; truncating small singular values gives the best low-rank approximation.
PCA keeps the top eigenvectors of the covariance matrix.

items: ELI5. An eigenvector is an arrow a machine only stretches and never turns. Imagine stirring paint: most of it swirls, but there is one line that just moves along. The SVD finds the most important stretches in any table of numbers.

A system of linear equations such as two x plus y equals five and x minus y equals one is the question: which vector x does the matrix A send to the vector b? If A is invertible there is exactly one answer.
Gaussian elimination finds it by adding multiples of one row to another until the matrix is triangular, then solving from the bottom up.

The determinant is a single number attached to a square matrix. For a two by two matrix it is a d minus b c. Geometrically it is the factor by which the map scales areas or volumes, with a sign for flipping. If it is zero the map squashes space onto something flatter and cannot be undone.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} \det\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix} = ad - bc, \\[0.6em] A v = \lambda v \iff \det(A - \lambda I) = 0 \end{gathered}

items: Most vectors change direction when a matrix acts on them, but some do not: they are only stretched. These are eigenvectors, and the stretch factor is the eigenvalue. They reveal the natural axes of a map.
Repeating the map many times makes any generic vector line up with the eigenvector of largest eigenvalue, which is the idea behind power iteration and Google's PageRank.
The singular value decomposition works for every matrix, not just square ones. It writes A as a rotation, a stretch along coordinate axes and another rotation. The stretches are the singular values.
Keeping only the largest few gives the best possible low-rank approximation, used to compress images and to find latent factors in data.

Principal component analysis applies this to data. Centre the data, compute its covariance matrix and take the eigenvectors with the largest eigenvalues. They are the directions of greatest spread, and projecting onto the first few gives a short summary of each point with minimal loss.

chapters.title: Calculus: limits, derivatives and the chain rule

maps.title: Calculus
links: Limit | describes | Behaviour near a point
Derivative | is | Instantaneous rate of change
Integral | accumulates | Area under a curve

summary: Calculus is the mathematics of change. The derivative of a function measures how fast its output changes as its input changes: the slope of the curve at a point. The integral adds up small pieces to find total change or area.

The chain rule differentiates a function of a function. It is the single most important rule for AI, because a neural network is a long composition of simple functions and backpropagation is the chain rule applied to it.
The labs estimate derivatives numerically, apply the rules, integrate by the trapezoid rule and build a Taylor approximation.

glossary.def: The value a function approaches as the input approaches a point.
f'(x) = lim (f(x+h) - f(x))/h.
(f g)' = f' g + f g'.
The accumulated area under a curve.
A polynomial approximation built from derivatives at a point.

keyPoints: d/dx x^n = n x^(n-1); d/dx e^x = e^x; d/dx ln x = 1/x.
Sum rule, product rule, quotient rule, chain rule.
Derivative of sigmoid: s'(x) = s(x)(1 - s(x)).
Fundamental theorem: the integral of f' from a to b equals f(b) - f(a).
Taylor: f(x+h) ~ f(x) + f'(x) h + f''(x) h^2/2.
At a minimum or maximum the derivative is zero.

items: ELI5. The derivative is the speedometer reading: how fast something changes right now. The chain rule says if gear A turns gear B and B turns C, the speed of C is the product of the gear ratios.

Imagine driving a car. Your position changes with time, and your speed is how fast. The derivative is exactly that: the instantaneous rate of change. To find it, take the change in output over a small change in input and let the input change shrink to zero.
The result is the slope of the tangent line.

A handful of rules give the derivative of almost everything. Derivatives of sums add; the product rule handles products; the chain rule handles functions inside functions. If y depends on u and u depends on x, then the rate of change of y with x is the product of the two rates.

Why does this matter for AI? A network computes a chain: input, layer one, layer two, and finally a loss. To learn, we need the slope of the loss with respect to every weight. The chain rule lets us multiply local slopes along the chain, one layer at a time. That is backpropagation.

The integral goes the other way. It sums many thin slices to give the area under a curve, and the fundamental theorem says that this equals the change in an antiderivative. In probability, integrals add up the chance over a range of values.
Finally, a Taylor series approximates a smooth function near a point by a polynomial, which explains why gradient methods work: near any point, a smooth function looks like a straight line.

chapters.title: Multivariate calculus: gradients, Jacobians and backpropagation

maps.title: Multivariate
links: Partial derivative | holds | Other variables fixed

summary: Functions in AI take many inputs, so we need derivatives in many dimensions. A partial derivative changes one variable and holds the others still. The gradient collects all partials into a vector pointing in the direction of steepest increase.

The Jacobian is the matrix of partials of a vector-valued function, and the Hessian is the matrix of second derivatives, describing curvature. The multivariate chain rule multiplies Jacobians, and backpropagation does it efficiently from the loss backwards.
The labs compute gradients, check them numerically, and run backpropagation through a tiny network.

glossary.def: df/dx_i: change in f when only x_i moves.
The vector of all partials; the direction of steepest ascent.
Matrix J_ij = d f_i / d x_j of a vector function.
Matrix of second partial derivatives.
Chain rule applied from the output to the inputs.
Compare analytic gradients with finite differences.

keyPoints: grad f = (df/dx1, ..., df/dxn); it is orthogonal to level sets.
Directional derivative = grad f . u for a unit vector u.
Chain rule: J of (f o g) = J_f J_g.
For a linear layer y = W x: dL/dW = (dL/dy) x^T and dL/dx = W^T (dL/dy).
Hessian positive definite means a local minimum at a critical point.
Reverse mode costs about the same as one forward pass for a scalar loss.

items: ELI5. The gradient is a compass that points straight uphill on a hill with many directions. Backpropagation is sending the blame for a wrong answer backwards through the machine, so each part knows how much it caused.
Take a hill. At any point, you could walk north, east, or any direction in between. The slope depends on the direction. A partial derivative is the slope when you walk strictly along one axis.
Put all the partials in a list and you have the gradient, which points straight uphill, and its length is how steep the hill is.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} \nabla f = \Bigl(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1},\dots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}\Bigr), \\[0.6em] D_u f = \nabla f \cdot u \end{gathered}

items: For a function whose output is also a vector, we stack the gradients of each output into the Jacobian matrix. It is the best linear approximation of the function near a point. Linear algebra and calculus meet here: locally, every smooth function acts like a matrix.

The chain rule becomes a product of Jacobians. In a network, the loss depends on the last layer, which depends on the one before, and so on. Computing the product from the loss backwards means each step is a vector times a matrix, which is cheap.
That is reverse-mode differentiation, or backpropagation. A single backward pass gives the gradient with respect to every weight.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} y = Wx \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{\partial L}{\partial W} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial y}\,x^{\top}, \\[0.6em] \frac{\partial L}{\partial x} = W^{\top}\frac{\partial L}{\partial y} \end{gathered}

items: The Hessian matrix of second derivatives describes curvature. At a point where the gradient is zero, a Hessian with all positive eigenvalues means a valley bottom, a local minimum. Mixed signs mean a saddle, which is common in the high-dimensional landscapes of deep learning.
A good habit is the gradient check: compare your formulas with small finite differences to catch bugs.

chapters.title: Optimization: gradient descent, convexity and Lagrange multipliers
summary: Training a model means minimising a loss. Gradient descent repeats a simple step: move a little against the gradient. The learning rate is the step size, and too large a step overshoots while too small a step crawls.

A convex function has a single valley, so descent finds the global minimum. Deep networks are not convex, yet descent works well in practice. Momentum, stochastic mini-batches and adaptive methods improve it. Lagrange multipliers handle constraints.
The labs run gradient descent, show how the step size matters, implement momentum and solve a constrained problem.

glossary.def: The function to minimise, such as a loss.
x <- x - lr * grad f(x).
The step size in gradient descent.
A function lying below its chords; every local minimum is global.
Keep a running average of past gradients.
Turns a constrained problem into an unconstrained one.

keyPoints: Update: x_{t+1} = x_t - eta * grad f(x_t).
For f = a x^2, descent converges when 0 < eta < 1/a.
Convex: f(tx + (1-t)y) <= t f(x) + (1-t) f(y).
Momentum: v <- beta v + grad; x <- x - eta v.
Constrained optimum: grad f = lambda grad g with g(x) = 0.
SGD uses a random mini-batch to estimate the gradient.

items: ELI5. Gradient descent is walking downhill in the fog by feeling the slope. Take small steps; too big and you leap over the valley. Constraints are fences: the best place is where the fence is parallel to the hill.

Picture standing on a foggy hillside, wanting the lowest point. You cannot see far, but you can feel the slope under your feet. So you step downhill, feel again, and repeat. That is gradient descent. Each step moves against the gradient by an amount set by the learning rate.

The learning rate matters a lot. For the simple bowl f equals a times x squared, steps smaller than one over a converge smoothly, steps near that size bounce, and larger steps blow up. In practice you tune it, or let methods such as Adam adapt it.

Convexity makes things easy. A convex function is shaped like a bowl: any line between two points on its graph lies above the graph. Every local minimum is then a global minimum, and descent cannot get trapped. Linear and logistic regression are convex.
Deep networks are not, but descent still finds good solutions.

Momentum adds memory: the update follows a running average of recent gradients, like a heavy ball rolling downhill, which smooths noise and speeds travel along narrow valleys. Stochastic gradient descent uses a small random batch of data at each step.
It is noisy but cheap, and the noise can even help escape poor spots.

Sometimes the answer must satisfy a rule. Lagrange multipliers handle equality constraints: at the best point, the gradient of the objective is parallel to the gradient of the constraint, so the objective cannot be improved without breaking the rule.
The multiplier says how much the optimum would change if the constraint were loosened.

chapters.title: Probability: axioms, conditional probability and Bayes' rule

maps.title: Probability
links: Event | is | A set of outcomes
Conditional | restricts to | What is known
Random variable | maps | Outcomes to numbers

summary: Probability measures uncertainty. A sample space lists all outcomes, an event is a set of them, and probability assigns a number between zero and one. The axioms make these numbers behave consistently.

Conditional probability asks: given that this happened, how likely is that? Independence means one event tells you nothing about the other. Bayes' rule reverses a conditional and is the engine of learning from evidence.
The labs compute conditional probabilities, apply Bayes to a medical test, check independence and simulate with a counting argument.

glossary.def: The set of all possible outcomes.
A subset of the sample space.
P(A | B) = P(A and B)/P(B).
P(A and B) = P(A) P(B).
P(A | B) = P(B | A) P(A) / P(B).
A number attached to each outcome.

keyPoints: Axioms: P(event) >= 0; P(whole space) = 1; probabilities of disjoint events add.
P(not A) = 1 - P(A); P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).
Law of total probability: P(B) = sum over i of P(B | A_i) P(A_i).
Bayes: posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior.
Independent events: P(A | B) = P(A).
Base-rate neglect: ignoring P(A) when reading a test result.

items: ELI5. Probability is a number from zero to one for how sure we are. Bayes' rule updates our belief when we see evidence. Remember that a rare disease stays rare even after a positive test, unless the test is truly excellent.

Roll a die. The sample space is the six faces. An event such as even is a set of faces, and its probability is the favourable outcomes over all outcomes when they are equally likely. The axioms say that probabilities are never negative, the whole space has probability one, and disjoint events add.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} P(A\mid B) = \frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}, \\[0.6em] P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\ \text{if independent} \end{gathered}

items: Conditioning changes the sample space. Knowing a die is even leaves three faces, so the chance of a six becomes one third. Two events are independent if knowing one does not change the chance of the other, such as two separate coin flips.

Bayes' rule turns a conditional around. We often know how likely a symptom is given a disease, but want to know how likely the disease is given the symptom. The rule combines the likelihood, the prior and a normaliser.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} P(H\mid E) = \frac{P(E\mid H)\,P(H)}{P(E)}, \\[0.6em] P(E)=\sum_i P(E\mid H_i)P(H_i) \end{gathered}

items: Imagine a disease that affects one person in a thousand, and a test that is ninety-nine percent accurate. A positive result does not mean a ninety-nine percent chance of illness.

Among a thousand people, one is ill and nearly always tests positive, but about ten of the healthy ones also test positive. So the chance is only about one in eleven. Forgetting the base rate is one of the most common reasoning errors.
A random variable assigns a number to each outcome, such as the sum of two dice. Almost all of machine learning treats data and predictions as random variables, and training as inference about them.

chapters.title: Random variables, distributions and expectation

maps.title: Distributions
links: Law of large numbers | says | Averages settle
Central limit theorem | explains | Why bells appear

summary: A random variable has a distribution: how likely each value is. The expectation is the average value, the variance measures spread and the standard deviation is its square root. Common distributions include Bernoulli, binomial, uniform and Gaussian.
Two theorems explain why statistics works. The law of large numbers says averages settle on the expectation. The central limit theorem says sums of many small independent effects look Gaussian.
The labs compute expectations and variances, evaluate the Gaussian density, compute binomial probabilities and simulate averages.

glossary.def: E[X] = sum x P(x): the probability-weighted average.
Var(X) = E[(X - mean)^2].
A single yes or no trial with success probability p.
The count of successes in n independent Bernoulli trials.
The bell curve with mean mu and standard deviation sigma.
Averages of many independent samples become Gaussian.

keyPoints: E[a X + b Y] = a E[X] + b E[Y] always (linearity).
Var(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2; Var(aX) = a^2 Var(X).
Binomial: P(k) = C(n, k) p^k (1-p)^(n-k); mean np, variance np(1-p).
Gaussian density: exp(-(x-mu)^2/(2 sigma^2)) / (sigma sqrt(2 pi)).
Law of large numbers: the sample mean tends to E[X].
CLT: the mean of n samples has standard deviation sigma/sqrt(n).

items: ELI5. A random variable is a number that depends on luck, like a die roll. The expectation is the long-run average. Add up many small random effects and the total always looks like a bell, which is why bells are everywhere.

A random variable is a number whose value depends on chance. Its distribution lists how likely each value is. For a fair die, each of one to six has probability one sixth. The expectation is the long-run average, found by weighting each value by its probability.

Expectation is linear: the expectation of a sum is the sum of expectations, even when the variables depend on each other. This simple fact solves many puzzles. Variance measures how far values typically stray from the mean; it adds for independent variables.

A Bernoulli variable is a single coin flip with chance p of success. The sum of n independent flips is binomial, with mean n p and variance n p times one minus p. The Gaussian, or normal, distribution is the bell curve described by a mean and a standard deviation.
Most of its mass lies within two standard deviations of the mean.
Why do bell curves appear everywhere? The central limit theorem says that the average of many independent random effects is approximately Gaussian, whatever the individual distributions.

The law of large numbers says that average settles toward the expectation as the sample grows, with spread shrinking like one over the square root of the sample size. This is why polls of a thousand people can be accurate, and why Gaussian noise is the default model in machine learning.

chapters.title: Statistics: estimation, likelihood and hypothesis tests

maps.title: Statistics
links: p-value | measures | Surprise under the null

summary: Statistics goes from data back to the world. We draw a sample and estimate properties of the population. The likelihood scores how well a parameter explains the data, and maximum likelihood picks the best parameter. A prior adds earlier belief, giving the MAP estimate.

A confidence interval says how precise an estimate is. A hypothesis test asks whether the data would be surprising if nothing were going on. The bias-variance trade-off explains overfitting and underfitting in machine learning.
The labs compute estimates, a maximum-likelihood coin bias, a confidence interval, a z statistic and a bias-variance example.

glossary.def: A rule that computes a parameter guess from data.
P(data | parameter) viewed as a function of the parameter.
The parameter value that maximises the likelihood.

keyPoints: Sample mean estimates the mean; sample variance divides by n - 1.
For a coin with k heads in n flips, the MLE of p is k/n.
95 percent interval for a mean: mean +/- 1.96 s/sqrt(n).
z = (mean - mu0) / (s / sqrt(n)).
MSE = bias^2 + variance (+ noise).
Least squares is the MLE under Gaussian noise.

items: ELI5. Statistics is detective work from clues. The likelihood asks which story makes the data least surprising. A simple story that misses details is biased; a story that memorises every detail is too jumpy to trust.

You cannot ask every voter, so you ask a sample and estimate. The sample mean is an estimator of the population mean. It is unbiased, and its error shrinks with the square root of the sample size. For the variance we divide by n minus one, which corrects for using the same data to find the mean.

The likelihood turns the question around. Fix the data and ask: how plausible is each value of the parameter? For a coin that gave seven heads in ten flips, the likelihood of a bias p peaks at p equals 0.7. Choosing the peak is maximum likelihood estimation.
Many familiar methods are special cases; least squares is maximum likelihood with Gaussian noise.

Adding a prior gives the maximum a posteriori estimate. A prior that prefers small weights turns into weight decay in neural networks. With little data the prior matters a lot; with lots of data the likelihood wins.

A confidence interval reports the precision of an estimate. For a mean it is the estimate plus or minus about two standard errors. A hypothesis test starts from a null, such as the new drug does nothing, and asks how surprising the data would be if it were true. A small p-value means surprising.
It does not give the probability that the null is true, a common mistake.

The bias-variance trade-off is the central idea of learning from data. A simple model is stable but may miss the pattern, which is bias. A flexible model fits the sample but changes wildly with new data, which is variance. Total error combines both. Good practice balances them using held-out data.

chapters.title: Information theory: entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence
summary: Information theory measures uncertainty and information in bits. A rare event is more surprising than a common one, so surprise is minus the log of the probability. Entropy is the average surprise of a distribution: how unpredictable it is.

Cross-entropy measures the cost of coding data from one distribution with a model of another, and is the standard loss for classifiers and language models. The KL divergence is the extra cost, a measure of how far a model is from the truth. Mutual information measures what two variables share.
The labs compute entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence and mutual information.

glossary.def: -log2 p(x) bits.
H(p) = -sum p log p.
H(p, q) = -sum p log q.
D(p || q) = sum p log (p/q) = H(p, q) - H(p).
I(X;Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X, Y).
The information in one fair yes-no answer.

keyPoints: A fair coin has entropy 1 bit; a certain event has 0.
Entropy is maximal for the uniform distribution: log2 n.
KL divergence is never negative and zero only when p = q.
KL is not symmetric: D(p||q) differs from D(q||p).
Minimising cross-entropy over q equals minimising KL to p.
Shannon: no lossless code beats the entropy on average.

items: ELI5. Information is surprise. A coin that always lands heads tells you nothing, so it has zero bits. Entropy is the average surprise. Cross-entropy is how surprised you are when you believed the wrong story.

Suppose someone tells you it rained in a desert. That is surprising, so it carries a lot of information. Learning that the sun rose tells you nothing. Shannon captured this: the information of an event with probability p is minus the log of p.
With base two logs it is measured in bits, the number of yes-no questions needed.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} H(p) = -\sum_x p(x)\log_2 p(x), \\[0.6em] H(p,q) = -\sum_x p(x)\log_2 q(x) \end{gathered}

items: Entropy is the average surprise: how many bits you need on average to say which outcome happened. A fair coin has one bit. A coin that is almost always heads has little. A uniform choice among n options has log of n bits, the most possible. Entropy is also a hard limit on lossless compression.

Now suppose reality follows p but you code using a model q. The average cost is the cross-entropy, which is always at least the entropy. Training a classifier or a language model with cross-entropy loss means making the model's distribution match the data. The excess cost is the KL divergence.

KL divergence is not a true distance, since it is not symmetric, but it is zero only when the distributions agree. It appears in variational autoencoders, in PPO's trust region and in DPO's regulariser.
Mutual information measures how much knowing one variable reduces uncertainty about another, the foundation of feature selection and representation learning.

summary: A Markov chain moves between states with fixed probabilities where the next state depends only on the current one. A transition matrix lists the probabilities, and multiplying a distribution by it advances one step.

Under mild conditions the chain forgets its start and settles into a stationary distribution. This idea gives PageRank, sampling methods such as MCMC, hidden Markov models and the Markov decision processes of reinforcement learning.
The labs step a chain, compute its stationary distribution by iteration, simulate a random walk exactly by enumeration and evaluate a small MDP value.

keyPoints: A distribution evolves by pi_{t+1} = pi_t P.
The stationary pi satisfies pi = pi P and sums to 1.

items: ELI5. A Markov chain is a board game where your next square depends only on the square you are on. Play for a very long time and the share of time on each square settles down, whatever square you started from.

Think of weather as sunny or rainy. If it is sunny today, there is a ninety percent chance of sun tomorrow; if rainy, a fifty percent chance of rain. Tomorrow depends only on today, not on last week. That memoryless rule is the Markov property.
The probabilities form a transition matrix whose rows each sum to one.

If you start with a distribution over states, multiplying by the matrix gives the distribution one step later. Do it repeatedly and, for a well-behaved chain, the distribution converges to a fixed one, the stationary distribution, no matter where you started.
It is the long-run share of time spent in each state.

A random walk on a graph, where you move to a random neighbour, is a Markov chain. PageRank models a web surfer who follows links at random and sometimes jumps to a random page; the stationary distribution ranks pages by how often the surfer visits.
Markov chain Monte Carlo reverses the idea: design a chain whose stationary distribution is one you want to sample.

Add actions and rewards and you get a Markov decision process, the model behind reinforcement learning. The value of a state is the best expected total discounted reward from it, satisfying the Bellman equation. Q-learning and PPO, met in earlier courses, are ways of solving it.

chapters.title: Algebra and category theory

maps.title: Algebra
links: Monoid | has | Associative product and identity

summary: Algebra studies structures with operations. A monoid has an associative operation and a do-nothing element; a group also has inverses. These abstract patterns appear all over computing: strings under concatenation, numbers under addition, permutations and symmetries.

Category theory goes one level up and studies structure by arrows alone. A category has objects and composable arrows. A functor maps one category to another preserving structure, which is exactly what a map over a list does. Monads package effects such as state and failure.
The labs check monoid and group laws, implement a functor on lists and options, compose arrows and build a tiny monad.

glossary.def: A set with an associative operation and an identity element.
A monoid in which every element has an inverse.
Objects, arrows, composition and identities.
A structure-preserving map between categories.
A functor with unit and bind, modelling computation with effects.
Characterising an object by how arrows relate to it.

keyPoints: Monoid laws: (a b) c = a (b c); e a = a e = a.
Group: every a has an inverse with a a^-1 = e.
Category: composition is associative; id composes neutrally.
Functor laws: F(id) = id; F(g o f) = F(g) o F(f).
Monad laws: left identity, right identity, associativity of bind.
Product and sum types are universal constructions.

items: ELI5. A group is a set of moves you can undo, like turning a Rubik's cube. A category is a map of dots and arrows that cares only about how arrows join. A functor translates one map into another while keeping the joins.

A monoid is a very simple idea: a way to combine things, where grouping does not matter, plus a neutral element. Adding numbers with zero, joining strings with the empty string, and merging lists all fit.
Because grouping does not matter, a monoid can be combined in parallel, which is why map-reduce works.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} (a\cdot b)\cdot c = a\cdot(b\cdot c), \\[0.6em] e\cdot a = a\cdot e = a \end{gathered}

items: A group adds inverses: every element can be undone. The symmetries of a shape, the rotations of a cube and the integers under addition are groups. Groups describe symmetry, and symmetry is behind convolutional networks, which share weights across positions, and equivariant networks.

A category is a collection of objects and arrows between them, where arrows compose and each object has an identity arrow. Sets and functions form a category; so do types and programs. The idea is to ignore what objects contain and study how they connect.
Two objects are the same, up to isomorphism, if there are arrows both ways that undo each other.

A functor maps a category into another, sending objects to objects and arrows to arrows, while respecting composition and identities. A list type with its map function is a functor: it turns a function from A to B into a function on lists of A to lists of B.
A natural transformation maps between functors, such as turning an option into a list.

A monad is a functor with two operations: wrap a plain value, and chain computations that return wrapped values. It captures effects such as possible failure, state, logging or probability, while keeping code composable.
A universal property defines something by how it relates to all others; the product of two types is the unique type with two projections.

chapters.title: Type theory and the lambda calculus
summary: The lambda calculus is the smallest programming language: just functions and application. A function is written with lambda, and applying it substitutes the argument. Everything computable can be expressed in it.

Types classify terms and rule out nonsense, like adding a string to a number. The Curry-Howard correspondence says types are propositions and programs are proofs. Dependent types let types mention values, and proof assistants use them to check mathematics by computer.
The labs evaluate lambda terms with Church numerals, type-check tiny expressions and implement a Boolean type.

glossary.def: A variable, a function (lambda x. body), or an application (f a).
(lambda x. t) a reduces to t with a for x.
A label saying what kind of value a term is.
The number n encoded as n-fold function application.
Propositions are types; proofs are programs.
A type that depends on a value.

keyPoints: Syntax: x | lambda x. t | t u.
Beta: (lambda x. t) u -> t[x := u].
Typing: if x : A and t : B then lambda x. t : A -> B.
Church numerals: n = lambda f. lambda x. f^n x.
A -> B reads as 'A implies B'; a pair type reads as 'and'; a sum type as 'or'.
Simply typed terms always terminate.

items: ELI5. The lambda calculus is a language with only recipes and swaps. A function is a recipe with a blank, and applying it fills the blank. Types are labels on boxes that stop you putting a square peg in a round hole. A proof is a program in disguise.

The lambda calculus has only three things: variables, functions and applications. A function that adds one is written lambda x dot x plus one. Applying it to three replaces x by three. This replacement is called beta reduction, and repeating it is how computation happens.
Remarkably, this tiny system can express every computable function.

Even numbers can be built from functions. The Church numeral for n is the function that applies another function n times. Addition and multiplication follow by composing these. Booleans work too: true picks the first of two choices and false picks the second.

Types make programs safer. A type says what kind of thing a term is; a function from A to B takes an A and gives a B. A type checker rejects terms that do not fit, such as applying a number as if it were a function.
In the simply typed calculus every well-typed program terminates, which is both a strength and a limit.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} \frac{x:A \vdash t:B}{\vdash \lambda x.\,t : A\to B}, \\[0.6em] \frac{\vdash f:A\to B \\[0.6em] \vdash a:A}{\vdash f\,a : B} \end{gathered}

items: Here is the deep connection. The rules above, read as logic, are the rules for implication: a function from A to B is a proof that A implies B, and applying it is modus ponens. A pair of values is a proof of and; a tagged choice is a proof of or.
This is the Curry-Howard correspondence, and it explains why running a program and simplifying a proof are the same process.

Dependent types go further by letting types mention values, such as a list of exactly n items. They can express precise specifications, and with them for all and there exists become types. Proof assistants such as Lean and Coq are built on this: if the proof type-checks, the theorem holds.
They have verified compilers, operating-system kernels and parts of modern mathematics.
